top_choice_rationale: Alexis Wright remains my first choice, as a close judgment of degree over Cărtărescu and Michon. The case rests on prose and structure, not on the political or cultural weight of the subject. Carpentaria and The Swan Book build large polyphonic narratives that take their architecture, handling of time and collective voice from Aboriginal oral practice. They hold sovereignty, memory and ecological catastrophe in one language, which I read as a formal departure inside English. The main weakness is the base for a whole-oeuvre citation. My knowledge of Praiseworthy, the nonfiction and Tracker is thinner and unverified, so I cannot confirm that the later work extends rather than restates the earlier method. I also cannot judge the oral register of her English from outside. Cărtărescu is my second choice because his longer record answers the sustained-quality worry more directly, and Palm's and Swärd's structural account of the change between Blinding and Solenoid is the strongest reply to the repetition concern, though it remains unverified. Michon is third: his consistency and sentence-level exactness are strong, but significance across a compact oeuvre is the harder criterion. Adonis ranks fourth only because I cannot assess the Arabic line or the later volumes without specialist reports, which are not in the files. That is a limit on my access, not a verdict on the poetry. Every candidate here has a serious literary case, so I place no award last. Translation and corpus-coverage uncertainties apply to all of them, and I have not independently verified any text.
recusal_note: None apparent from the profile: no connection to any shortlisted writer is recorded. Context only, not evidence of preference: she is Permanent Secretary and co-opted member (whether a co-opted member votes is undocumented, so this vote is a modeling assumption), was elected alongside Steve Sem-Sandberg in 2020, is married to Pär Nuder, and works in literary non-fiction.
